review:
The Ultimate Time-Gated Time Sink.

Great setting, pretty good gameplay. This is not a traditional 'action-adventure rpg'. This is like a single-player MMO. The setting is beautiful and there's lots of exploration. And, it's free.

However here's what you need to know before investing your time.

Progression is time-gated. You can only level your character so many times before needing to 'breakthrough' to the next tier. These breakthroughs are time gated. The first couple are once a day. But at level 40, I now have to wait two days before I can 'breakthrough' and level again. All xp gained in the meantime is 'stored' until your next breakthrough. The bigger problem is that many quests, the ability to progress 'the story' and move to different areas, are dependent on your level.

EDIT: I'm seeing from a lot of people that the time-gates are a temporary part of the season, I hope this is true.

Now lets talk about the Wuxia gameplay elements. The cinematics in this game are cool. And the combat system is alright -everything looks cool, but it requires more thumbs if you're playing with controller. The gameplay is nowhere near as simple as the previews make it look. As for the 'flying kung fu' that fans love... it's not available until you've explored most of a given map.... which is self-defeating to say the least. It's also extremely janky and you can't really control it, just basically which general direction you want to go. There are other less overt 'Lightness' skills like wall striding, running fast, running across water, etc. However, for most quests you can't use any of these skills. All the Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon stuff seems to be for exploration only. It's extremely jarring and immersion-breaking when you're exploring the world and all of the sudden you're grounded to bunny hops because you found yourself in a quest area.

The last thing you need to know, is that this game is tucked inside a menu simulator. There are menus within menus within menus. There is an enormous amount of tracked challenges, collectibles, resources, skills, talents, shops, events, etc to unlock. This thing is a lot like an MMO. I started having flashbacks to Warframe with the ungodly amount of resources and various things to 'level up'. You have to level up your character, your gear, your martial arts, your mystic ways, inner ways, harmony, your profession, your profession's skills, and no I'm not even kidding -even your gear slots. The main reason this is billed as an rpg is because there is a singular story arc specific to your character.

But hey, it's free. The game is beautiful. The boss fights and cinematics are cool. I nearly shed a tear during the Velvet Shade's Revelry Hall cinematic. The game shoots itself in the foot on a few things, but I'm enjoying it. It's loads of free content that's obviously kept me entertained many hours.

At first I wasn’t really sure what to think about this game. A F2P RPG with no P2W sounds way too good in 2025, so I expected another forgettable game, but it honestly surprised me in a good way.

The F2P model is very clean. Everything you can buy is cosmetic and the battle pass is also purely cosmetic. There’s no P2W at all, which is still rare these days. The only thing some people might consider “P2W” are the mounts you can buy in the cash shop, since they gather resources for you, but honestly the impact is very small, so it feels more like a QoL feature than anything else.

The first thing you need to know is that this is not an MMO, even if it has an “MMO mode” with world bosses, dungeons, GvG and online activities. The core of the game is an open world RPG with lots of systems, minigames and small interactions everywhere. There’s also a co-op mode, but this one is only for exploring, doing side missions and other activities together. The main story is singleplayer.

The combat feels good, dynamic and fluid. You combine two weapons and play classic archetypes like tank, melee DPS, ranged DPS or even healer. There’s no upgrade system based on probabilities. You simply get the materials and level up your gear in a consistent way. You also have mystical abilities on top of your weapon skills, plus a talent tree, although it’s a simple one.

For PvP you get a 1v1 arena, a 50-player battleroyale-style mode, duels and GvG.

One interesting feature is the AI chat system, which lets you gain friendship with NPCs. It’s pretty basic, don’t expect deep conversations, but it’s well integrated and helps you unlock tasks and extra rewards. Some NPCs can give you items if you listen to what they say and help them, even though they don’t have markers or indicators. It adds a nice sense of discovery.

There are also a lot of activities: the jar game, dialectic duels, musical minigames, puzzles and many small things that make the world feel alive. You can play most of these with friends. On the first day I played a card game similar to “liar’s dice” with several friends. We had a good laugh and even leveled up a couple of times.

The game can run on both DirectX 11 and DirectX 12, but it’s clearly better on 12, with frame generation and more consistent visuals. So make sure to select the right option on Steam when you launch the game. (A small window appears when you click play, so it’s easy to find.)

It also has tutorials for almost everything. Each system, mechanic and feature is explained, so it’s hard to get lost even with the amount of things the game offers.

The biggest issue when you start is the number of menus and different currencies you get. Even though the menus unlock progressively, the first hours can be a bit confusing, but you get used to it after playing for a while. Some translations are also a bit rough and need to be polished, but it’s not a big deal.

In short, Where Winds Meet is a F2P RPG that really surprises. It offers a world full of activities, fun combat and an online mode that, while not a real MMO, adds variety without making things complicated. If you enjoy RPGs with tons of things to do and no pressure to spend money, give it a try. I’m pretty sure you’ll like it.

[h1]One of the most ambitious games I've ever played[/h1]
Where Winds Meet is a wild game. I don't think I've ever seen a game where you can roleplay as a villain and go around killing NPCs, have bounties placed on you, get hunted by other players, get jailed if you get caught, and then to cut your sentence short, get paraded around town while other players hurl cabbages and eggs at you.
Oh, and this game also has raids, pvp, and a whole ass battle royale system built into it. This game tries to do a bit of everything and amazingly, it kinda pulls it off!

There's enough content packed into this one game that anyone should be able to find something they like. Don't want to fight? Just explore, take screenshots, play musical instruments (players have figured out Linkin Park on the Guzheng), heal NPCs or other players, dance, wrestle, play chess, quiz, wrestle, [b]build houses[/b]... the list goes on. 
Want hardcore fights? Fight challenging bosses solo or co-op (Legend difficulty is no joke), take out enemy camps head on or stealthily, tune your gear, experiment with different builds, join raids etc...

You get the idea. There is a ridiculous number of things you can do in this game. And it's all [b]free[/b], so what's there to lose by giving it a try?

After around 150 hours in this game, i think I'm qualified to write an actual review here.

First things first. As a souls player who loves the challenge, is this game worth your time? No.
Don't get me wrong. It DOES have challenging parts and challenges, but it isn't a souls game. Even as a souls-like, it's definitely on the easier side of games, which makes sense since it's ment to attract casual gamers who want to play with their friends as well. So, if you're a souls veteran who wants the hardest challenges there are, you'll be disappointed with this. Anyone else - Come in!

It also isn't your typical MMORPG. Yes, it does have MMO aspects, but for like 90% of your progress, you stay offline and explore your world, do story quests etc. You CAN play with friends to boost your exploration progress together, at the same time, which is huge. But, story missions are the ones you can not play in co-op, sorry guys. The "online mode" also isn't like a big open map with enemies everywhere for people to slay, no. It's more of a hub. Like, a lobby for players to meet and make up parties who then go into someones individual world together, or to form up for raids.

It's also not your typical F2P game. Buying the battlepass DOES grant you a small advantage, yes. But, it's basically almost meaningless, and all you can truly do with real money is buying cosmetics. This game isn't Pay 2 Win, it's essentially Pay 2 Flex. I am F2P with a 0.90€ cosmetic, not a single battlepass, and my power level is close to 20k at this point, which puts me above basically 99% of the players at the point of writing this. Individual skill also matters a lot more than gear in most cases, unless the difference in gear is extreme.

Progression is quite fast. A friend of mine who started just 2 weeks ago caught up with us day 1 endgame players already, currently at 17k power, and max level on their account. The game is time efficient, beginner friendly and honestly optimized pretty well.

Now, the negatives. As long as you're offline, everything is fine, crisp, and responsive. As soon as you play with others, however, expect massive desync and input lag. Me and my friends live close to each other, we all have a ping of between 5 and 20 - and still, no matter who's world we join, there's massive delays. The servers definitely are on the lower end of things I've seen within 20+ years of gaming, but that's something that could always change in the future.

All in all, the game is a solid 8/10. It's a F2P game that doesn't offer huge advantages from spending money. The gameplay is satisfactory and the progression is very good. However, there's negatives, like the poor server performance and a pretty weak main story plot (as of now). All fixable, of course. If you like souls like games but aren't one of these basement dwellers who need it to be the be-all end-all of souls likes, you'll love this game, especially with friends to play with. Even if you're a casual player who can't get their footing into souls games, this game might be for you. It's easier than most of them, it's online meaning your friends can help you get into it, and the only difficult part is learning and understanding the stats system of this game. But, YouTube is your friend, and with the willingness to look things up here and there, it won't be too much of an issue.

I have to say though, the translation is terrible in some places, but that does lead to some funny moments. "Look, so many money!"

My first hours in this game were an unhinged sitcom starring me, a bear, and several medical emergencies. 

I began by crafting a character so horrifying the character creator begged for mercy and the game politely pretended he was normal. Cutscenes paired my goblin-faced mess with perfect K-pop angel NPCs like a before-and-after skincare ad. It only got worse from there.

I witnessed a bear practicing tai chi to steal a beehive, copied the move like a shameless tourist, and immediately punted the bear into the sky like a furry space program. Bees then proceeded to dismantle my will to live, leaving me bruised, poisoned, and looking like expired fruit.

I accidentally stole a horse, got clotheslined by its previous owner, and realized I was one more injury away from becoming medically classified as soup.

Then salvation arrived, a stranger joined my session. His name might as well have been Asian John Wick. He rolled in, healed my collection of crippling ailments, bowed politely and then beat me into paste. Never took a scratch. Left like Batman.

I was humbled. Enlightened. Traumatized. And inspired.

Thus began my medical career.

I healed geese. I cured villagers. I stress-tested guildmates by practicing chakra healing on them at random intervals like an overly enthusiastic chiropractor. Eventually, I was curing depression, bone fractures, and probably childhood trauma.

Requests poured in endlessly. World chat named me The Green-Faced Duelist Doctor, the healer who cures first and challenges later. A legend with 100 flawless medical-violence house calls.

Then he returned.
The one who birthed my journey... Asian John Wick.

He asked me to cure a Soul Bind. I succeeded. We fought. I won with a single HP left and the spirit of every goose I ever healed behind me. He bowed one final time and vanished.

I sat there realizing: I have become the monster healer I feared.

Best free game ever.

It’s not often I play a free game and don’t feel like it’s quietly checking my credit score in the background. But Where Winds Meet? It actually feels… generous. Which is wild. Most “free-to-play” games start friendly and then slowly turn into a toll booth. This one honestly feels better than a bunch of $60 AAA titles I’ve bought, played for a week, and then quietly uninstalled.

Now, if you’re anything like me and the word “multiplayer” makes your blood pressure tick up a little, you’ll get this. I love big, living worlds. I do not love the idea of being the guy who wipes a 10-person raid and gets that long, awkward silence in chat. Instant alt-F4 energy.

This game fixes that.

The absolute MVP feature for me is Solo Mode. You can do almost everything in your own private instance. Just you, the scenery, and whatever poor boss is about to catch a sword to the face. For tougher fights, you bring AI companions. Are they elite esports champions? No. Do they stand in fire sometimes? Yep. But they get the job done and, more importantly, they don’t judge you. No pressure. No random stranger sighing into their mic. It makes the whole experience feel way more welcoming than most MMOs for someone like me.

What surprised me is that the game still gently nudges you toward other players without shoving you off a cliff. When I finally dipped a toe into multiplayer, it was… chill. Like, suspiciously chill.

Guilds are actually built around different playstyles. Want to explore? Fight other players? LARP as a traveling musician or doctor? There’s a lane for that. Honestly, the rewards alone make joining worth joining a guild (or even switching between them for the unique rewards in each). And co-op is another sweet spot. One or two other humans exploring together is manageable. Ten is a committee meeting. Small group content feels relaxed, and it makes special events way easier without turning the game into a part-time job.

There’s also always something going on. Daily and weekly stuff keeps you moving, and it feels like there’s constantly some event happening. The world never really feels dead.

And let me be clear: this is not pay-to-win. You don’t need to spend money to compete or succeed. Most of the paid stuff is cosmetic, which is fine. If someone wants to spend money to look like a legendary silk-robed demigod, good for them. There’s a monthly pass that speeds up materials a bit, but it’s optional. If you’ve got patience, you can earn everything (that matters for play) just by playing.

I haven’t run into toxicity or cheating, though I also avoid the ultra-hardcore PvP and multiplayer stuff, so your mileage may vary. But if you want a gorgeous, sprawling martial arts epic and you’re allergic to forced social chaos, this is absolutely worth a try.

[h1] Honest Review After 500+ Hours (Long Read) [/h1]

I have tried every aspect of this game 100% progress in some things, tried both high end pvp and leaderboard rankings. So here's an honest truth about the game. A wuxia styled F2P MMORPG with insane potential, beautiful worldbuilding, very similar to Wukong and Sekiro/Dark souls elements mixed in.

[h2] Customization [/h2]  
The character creator is [b]insanely detailed[/b] easily one of the best parts of the game. You can tweak faces to perfection and create almost any look you want.
However, it’s limited:
• No body customization (height, build, proportions locked)
• Only face + skin tone customization

You can look unique but only from the neck up.

[h2] Animation & Movement [/h2]
Movement is smooth, sprinting, parkour, climbing everything feels fluid.
You can climb trees, mountains, buildings basically anything if you have stamina.

[h2] Photo Mode [/h2]
The photo mode in this game is [b] insanely good [/b] and honestly one of the most underrated features.  
It offers:
• Advanced camera controls  
• Lighting adjustments (intensity, direction, tone)  
• Depth of field and focus tweaks  
• Filters and color grading  
• Pose and angle control
• Also newly added custom poses and dancing by tracing with AI from a source

[h2] Weapons & Combat [/h2]  
Huge variety of weapons:  
• Dual blades  
• Umbrellas  
• Spears  
• Katanas  
• And more  

Each weapon has its own:  
• Unique mechanics  
• Combos  
• Playstyle identity  
• Role in team fights  

[b] No weapon feels useless [/b] but here’s the catch:  
At high end PvP or leaderboard play, the meta becomes extremely narrow.  
If you want to compete, you’re forced into specific builds and weapon combinations. Freedom exists — until you want to be competitive.

[h3] Playstyles [/h3]  
Three main roles:  
• DPS  
• Healer  
• Tank  

These can be mixed depending on your build.  
Each role comes with:  
• Unique abilities  
• Combo systems  
• Team synergy 
You can also freely re-spec your gear if you get tired of 1 playstyle but limited amount of times in a season

[h2] World Building (best part) [/h2]  
The world is:  
• Beautiful
• Deeply inspired by Chinese history, folklore, and legends  
• Filled with handcrafted environments  

You’ll find:  
• Unique dungeons and cave systems  
• Massive mountains to climb  
• Fully interactive NPCs 
• Animals (cats, dogs, etc.)  
• Even AI NPC-chatbots

Every location feels carefully crafted and alive.

[h3] Exploration [/h3]  
Exploration is heavily rewarded so try and reach 100% for each part of the map, you will get:  
• Hidden loot  
• Lore  
• Character progression buffs  

There’s also a compendium system that tracks everything you discover from plants to NPCs, bosses etc.  

[h2] Social Features [/h2]  
This is one of the most social MMOs out there.

You can:  
• Hire players (healers, scholars)  
• Place bounties on players  
• Help others through bounty systems  
• Become a disciple or mentor  
• Form sworn groups  
• Get married/build relationships  
• Break players out of prison or capture them  
• Join guilds and sects  
• Play minigames  
• Dance, play instruments, relax in saunas

The game is designed to reward social interaction heavily with most cosmetics rewards behind it.

[h2] F2P & Monetization [/h2]  
The good 
• No pay to win 
• Gear cannot be bought with real money  
• Cosmetics can be earned in game  
• Free gacha pulls exist with guaranteed rewards over time  

The bad
• Gacha is extremely expensive (150–300$ for premium cosmetics)  
• Strong FOMO elements  
• Global version lacks trading systems (like China's Black Market)  

[h3] Cosmetics [/h3]  
Very different from western MMOs:  
• No oversexualized designs  
• Modest, elegant, wuxia style outfits  
• Unique designs for male/female  
• Full dye system  

[h2] Voice Acting & Translations [/h2]  
This is one of the weakest aspects:  
• Poor English voice acting  
• Missing or broken translations  
• Some things remains in Chinese  

[b] Recommendation: [/b] Play in Chinese with subtitles but even those aren't perfect.

[h2] Now for the bad part [/h2]
Since I mentioned a lot of pros here are the cons and why it's primarily bad and might affect current and future players

[b] 1. Timegated Progression [/b]  
You hit caps and must wait 1-3 weeks for breakthroughs.  
No grinding your way forward you’re forced to wait.

[b] 2. Global vs China Version [/b]  
China gets:  
• Better QoL  
• Better pricing for gacha 
• More features  

[b] 3. Gacha & Pricing [/b]  
• Extremely expensive  
• Worse pricing than Chinese version  
• Encourages FOMO heavily  

[b] 4. No Black market [/b] 
No trading system like China's Black Market less player freedom, more monetization pressure.

[b] 5. Server Issues [/b]  
The game only has 4 dedicated server locations
• Players will lag and affect others gameplay
• Host based sessions

[b] 6. Meta Problems [/b]

Where Winds Meet (WWM) is a Chinese action RPG game with a heavily inspired Wuxia setting. This is a sort of “Lobby-based’ MMO-lite where you can play solo or online with others. This is not a true Massively Multiplayer Online game - you won’t see hundreds of people at once. Instead, you have the option to complete PVE content with players, like boss fights, or play solo player, where the majority of the game is focused on. 
Despite the single player focus, I really like how WWM incorporates online aspects into the game. Whether it's through world chat, Dark Souls-like sign posts, or joining groups for healing/cultivation, there’s enough of a community focus where I never really felt alone. 

WWM is built around exploration, which greatly appealed to me. I found myself taking much longer to get from point A to B due to being constantly distracted by the amazing world and exploration. There are frequent mini-games and rewards for exploring that not only give you currency, but also develop your character by providing stat bonuses and improvements. 

Overall, I do recommend WWM. Despite some translation issues, this is a bona fide AAA-game that is free, respects players time, and is not P2W. I can see some issues in getting past the Chinese culture, translations, and I do question the longevity of the end game, but this is an experience and world absolutely worth spending some (free!) time in.

Overall, Where Winds Meet delivers a very satisfying experience in terms of gameplay, music, story, and especially visuals. The world design and artistic direction are genuinely impressive and help the game stand out in the MMORPG genre.

Despite being an MMORPG, it avoids pay-to-win mechanics. All purchases are purely cosmetic, which is a model I genuinely think other games in the genre should follow. It creates a fair environment where progression depends on your time and skill rather than your wallet.

The large open world and the typical in-game energy system can naturally push you toward extended play sessions and a fairly intense grind loop. However, thanks to the separate PvE mode and the currently available main story questline, players who are mainly interested in the narrative can get around 40–50 hours of satisfying content in its current state.

At the moment, the biggest downside is that the main story is not yet fully completed. That said, the game is actively updated with new regions, weapons, combat styles, and additional main story quests. If you are planning to play purely for the story and don’t enjoy returning to games later, I would recommend waiting until the narrative is more complete.

On the other hand, I can confidently say that the online elements are highly enjoyable and immersive.

Considering that the game is free, what we have here is a rare gem. If you’re looking to have a great time and enjoy an immersive world—especially with friends—Where Winds Meet is definitely worth checking out.

"Where Winds Meet" Essential Guide — From a 600-Hour (and counting) Chinese Player

First, please excuse my English — I'm writing this using AI translation. But as a Day 1 Chinese server player (Character UID: 0105284840 — this game has a separate Chinese client from the global one, that's why my hours in review doesn't reflect my actual play time, with that in mind please ignore my Steam playtime), after reading hundreds of reviews in various languages, I noticed many misunderstandings. That's why I specifically used a Hong Kong server account (the international version blocks mainland China IPs) to explain several common points of contention and try to help you understand this game:

1. 【P2W?】
Let's be clear first: No. The battle pass only increases potion carrying capacity — useless in PvP, somewhat useful in PvE but not impactful, because the most important things in it are the included gacha tickets and outfits. Besides the battle pass, you can also exchange 【First Clear of Strongholds(Medicinal Tales)】 rewards to increase potion carrying limits (current Chinese server cap is 7 bottles).
Of course, I understand spending habits may differ by region. If a $10 seasonal battle pass makes you feel like fighting NPCs is P2W, then I suggest lowering the game difficulty. That way you can win more, because you can save on potion materials, save time collecting materials, and save crafting gold.

2. 【Cash Shop】
As a free-to-play game, it needs to make money, but I think what you really want to know is: 【As a casual player, spending little or even nothing, can I get cool items?】 The answer is definitely YES.
—2.1 【Cash Prize Pools】
Quests give a small number of draw tickets (e.g., 1v1 duels with NPCs), and the developers also give some away. Accumulate for 6-8 months and you can get an outfit worth $500 for free (I got one for free). Please note: this pool is meant for players with money to spend(whales), not for casual players. This pool is key to keeping this game running!
—2.2 【Seasonal Prize Pools】
The green currency in the top-right corner of the interface can be exchanged for draw tickets. This currency is obtained through all gameplay activities: gathering / opening chests / quests / collections... (Acquisition speed is related to exploration progress. I've obtained it for free twice).
—2.3 【Direct Purchase Shop for Casual Players】
Item prices range from $1-40. I think the pricing is reasonable. If you still find it expensive, the daily login rewards include 1-2 "10% off" coupons per month. You can stack up to 5. As long as you have patience, you can get items for half price.
PS: Thanks to all the big spenders in the 【Cash Prize Pools】! You let us play a good game for free

3. 【Voice Acting】
If English dubbing isn't a must, I strongly recommend using the Chinese voiceover! I think the English dub quality is indeed subpar; the Chinese dub has better voice actors and emotional delivery. I also strongly advise against skipping the story — this is a masterpiece of a narrative. If you just want mindless combat, you might as well go play 《Naraka: Bladepoint》 directly.

4. 【Story】
Don't give a negative review just because a character diesthe game is set in an era of war and famine, where tragedies like "swapping children to eat" were common. In this desperate setting, any character's death is an inevitability of the times.

5. 【Quests & Quest Comment Section】
You can find in your exploration log that quests are divided into two lines. Many people haven't noticed this. One line is the overt main story, told through cinematic narration. The other is a hidden, fragmented narrative. The two lines converge into the complete plot and unlock the final storyline.After completing certain quests, a comment section opens. I strongly recommend reading it — even as a Chinese server player, I often gain new insights into the story from "history fan" comments!

6. 【Currency System】
Many players complain there are too many currency types and are confused why each map has different currencies (except the shop currency). First, the reason: different gameplay categories earn different currencies. It ensures players with different playstyles get corresponding rewards. Second, why do map currencies differ? Because the game is set during the transition between the Tang and Song dynasties in China, when multiple currencies circulated in parallel. As the main story reveals — when dynasties change, common people's lifelong savings often turn to nothing.

7. 【Road Signs & Chat Box】
You can customize in settings: display of road signs / chat box / flying chat messages. Solo players can also get a clean experience. (The chat box settings are within the chat box itself, not in the ESC settings.)

8. 【Mount System】
unless you really like them. Your parkour (Lightness skill) is far more powerful than any mount. If you want a functional mount, then 【Gathering】 and 【Treasure Chest Finding】 mounts are somewhat useful, making things a bit easier for you. But honestly, they're not as good as doing it yourself. The 【Sprint】 mount in the shop is decent: 1. cheap, 2. it has the fastest startup speed before you have parkour, even though it's still "slow". The reason mounts feel "slow" is because at low exploration levels, collectibles are very dense, so you don't want to repeatedly mount and dismount.

9. 【Parkour (Lightness skill) Adjustment】
Be sure to switch to another camera mode in the settings! It greatly improves the flying experience, so you don't have to keep watching that close-up animation!!! (Wind Rider is the highest and farthest, recommended.)

10. 【Multiplayer Modes】
I don't think this is a good MMO; I think it can only be called 【Co-op】. Actually, it leans more towards a single-player game, but I'll still explain the difference.
—Solo Mode: Up to 5-player co-op. Quest progress is NOT shared (similar to GW2's personal story). Exploration rewards & world boss kills within 300m are shared by the party.
—Multiplayer Mode: Reduced number of NPCs, cannot complete quests. Contains exclusive content like cruise parties.

11. 【Network Latency】
The developers are optimizing it, but I don't think it will improve much. Because as a Chinese player who has played foreign games for years, I know how terrible latency can be. Unless someone is willing to act as a local agent for this game and set up servers locally.

12. 【Inventory System】
Abandon your habit of organizing your inventory from MMOs! Don't try to organize your bag. What you should do is forget its existence, unless you pick up a letter and want to read its contents, or if you miss the pop-up notification when picking up an equipment chest. Otherwise, there's no need for you to organize anything. When you need to use something, that interface will automatically fetch items from your bag.

Finally, if you have other questions, feel free to leave a comment. I'll try my best to help.

[h1]Where Winds Meet – A Free Game That Surprised Me in the Best Way[/h1]

I went in with the mindset of avoiding online free games, mainly because many of them end up turning into pay-to-win or heavy grind traps. But after seeing a few reviews saying “just try it, it is free,” I gave it a chance.  
And honestly, I was shocked by how good it turned out.

People compare it to Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, Black Myth, and Sekiro.  
I only know the first two, but even then the comparisons make sense.  
The visuals instantly reminded me of Ghost of Tsushima’s atmosphere, especially during key story moments.

[h2]Story and Emotional Moments[/h2]

I did not expect a free game to hit this hard, especially so early on.

[spoiler]The ending of Chapter 1 genuinely caught me emotionally. It set the tone for the rest of the journey and felt far better than many paid games I played this year.
[/spoiler]

Chapter 2 also had one of my favourite twists:

[spoiler]Little Fu saying “I’m the Dao Lord,” then switching to “I work for the Dao Lord,” had everyone confused. And when the truth came out at the end, I laughed so hard because the community reaction online was exactly the same as mine.
[/spoiler]

Only two chapters are available right now, but both have solid closure and feel complete on their own.

[h2]Gameplay, UI, and World Feel[/h2]

Combat feels smooth once you learn enemy patterns. Some boss fights look incredible, especially for a free game.  
One side-boss took me hours, but once I learned everything, beating it felt extremely satisfying.

The UI can look busy at first, especially if you prefer clean single-player setups.  
Thankfully, you can hide almost everything in the settings and even turn off world chat on the side.

The world itself looks beautiful. The colours, animations, and overall presentation reminded me of modern AAA titles.

[h2]Online System and Why Everything Is Connected[/h2]

The game is always online, but the reason seems to be tied to how saves and progression work.  
From what I understand, saves are on the server possibly to prevent people from modifying files and skipping progression.  
At the same time, it looks like the developers wanted all modes — solo, co-op, and multiplayer — to share one character with the same stats.

I personally do not know the full technical reason, but that feels like the intention.  
It also means maintenance time can stop you from playing, which might feel odd if you prefer purely offline story games.

[h2]Progression, Resources, and Level Gates[/h2]

There are level gates. For example, to begin Chapter 2 you need to be level thirty.  
At first, I thought it would feel like a wall, but by the time I finished Chapter 1 I was already level twenty-eight.  
Doing two side missions pushed me to thirty, so it did not waste my time.

The only thing that bothered me slightly is how healing items and resources do not reset when you reload a save, since everything is online.  
If you run out of medicine, you have to go farm more and come back.  
Not a dealbreaker, but something to be aware of.

[h2]Monetisation and What You Actually Need[/h2]

The game mainly sells skins and a battle pass. The cosmetics do not give big stat advantages, and you can play smoothly without spending.  
Grinding is enough to keep up with main story requirements.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Even though only two chapters exist at the moment, both are strong and enjoyable.  
The world looks beautiful, the story has emotion and twists, and the combat impressed me far more than I expected from a free title.

It is one of those games where the phrase “just try it, love or hate, up to you” actually fits perfectly.

I honestly don’t understand how this game is free. Where Winds Meet feels like the kind of project where someone should be knocking on my door to charge me for “unauthorized enjoyment.” It’s one of the most generous free titles I’ve touched in years. 

The opening hours hit like a tidal wave. The game throws an entire arsenal of systems at you combat styles, cultivation abilities, mobility techniques, crafting, hunting, stealth, exploration tools, even social interactions and it doesn’t always do the best job explaining any of them. About two hours in, I was confused but also curious, because the game practically encourages you to poke around and discover things through trial and error. The learning curve is steep, but once you start piecing things together, the freedom becomes the appeal. The game leans hard into those classic Asian design sensibilities layered mechanics, busy UI, fast pacing which gives it personality, even if it’s a lot to absorb at first.

Combat is good, even if it’s not quite the Sekiro like precision some people expected. The auto parry system is a bit cheap in my opinion (thankfully you can disable it), but the real strength here is the variety. There are tons of weapons, martial arts disciplines, stances, and movement abilities that let you build your character in wild ways. The combat sandbox is flexable, you can double jump off projectiles, redirect arrows, kick enemies across rooftops, or switch from elegant swordplay to brutal spear combos. It’s not the deepest combat in the genre, but it’s creative and satisfying.

This is where the game starts feeling suspiciously premium. The cutscenes are shockingly well produced great direction, expressive facial animation, and a level of polish I didn’t expect for a free to play title. The world itself is gorgeous, full of scenic landscapes and small environmental details that make exploration feel rewarding. A common point from other reviews is that the world feels alive, with random events, wildlife, hidden quests, parkour routes, and interactable objects everywhere. It’s the kind of world design western studios used to be known for, but haven’t delivered consistently in years.

I was genuinely surprised by how much cosmetic content you get just by playing. Outfits, dyes, accessories far more than I expected, and without feeling nickel-and-dimed. The game is surprisingly fair, especially compared to the usual F2P model.

Asia has been on a massive upswing with recent releases, and Where Winds Meet continues that trend. It’s no surprise that western gamers are migrating toward these titles these developers seem hungry, creative, and connected to their audience in a way many western studios have drifted away from. Is the game perfect? No. It’s messy, overwhelming, inconsistent, and sometimes unpolished. But it’s also bold, stylish, generous, and packed with ideas more than most full-priced games offer. For an open-world martial arts adventure? It’s one of the most interesting ones in years.

Where Winds Meet (WWM) is an open world RPG set in a Chinese martial arts world with light fantasy elements. The game offers a huge map with many activities, such as mobs, bosses, treasures, puzzles, mini games, side quests and obviously also a main story. The combat is souls-light with a focus on getting parries and dodges right to counter for massive damage. While WWM feels to me like a fully-fledged single player game, it also has several multi-player features, such as dungeon and boss raids, pvp or social aspects (join a sect, perform daily tasks, get married, post a bounty on another random player, etc.).

WWM is "free to play" and currently entirely financed through battle passes and cosmetics. So far my anti-virus software has not yet detected any suspicious data mining activities ... The battle pass speeds up progression and grants some usually "no luck"-gatcha pulls for mid-tier cosmetics. The online features are meant to incentivize people to spend serious cash for the more "extravagant cosmetics".

I recommend this game to people who enjoy exploring beautiful open worlds with a broad range of activities. I am having fun playing WWM and it looks amazing! Not all is perfect though, as in order to manage your character and catch up on your next endeavour, you will have to navigate an impressively complex menu system. I am not exaggerating when I say, that it took me several hours to understand what I need to click and in which order to get things done. In a way it is somehow the boss I struggle most so far. I also seem to have a bit more of a hard time in this game to get the parries right. For the time being, I shall not blame network code as it is certainly a "me problem" ...

This game tries to do allot of different things, but it has a consistent theme across all its systems. Imagine you’re a famous painter, you’ve painted a masterpiece. A work of art. A mere glance at it dazzles the eyes. And then you draw a gigantic red line through the painting. Why? Who knows. Now, instead of trying to paint over that red line and fix the drawing, you offer people temporary glasses that hide the color red every time they view it. A band-aid solution to something you’ve done intentionally, with no benefit to you, only harm.
This is Where the Winds Meet.

Let me break down the systems of the game, as well as its pros and cons, to show you the marred painting I mean. I’ll try to keep it organized into systems and subsystems.

The Combat:
At a glance, combat seems very fun in WWM. It’s flashy, parry-based, all weapons have their own playstyle and combinations, and you can mix and match! Not really.
As you go deeper, you realize every “combo” is a reskin of the same style, with very few exceptions. Almost every available combination boils down to “this is your main weapon, use it 24/7” and “this is your secondary weapon, used only for a single ability or buff/debuff.”

You’re not really using both. Every build boils down to a 10–15 second buff/debuff window while spamming 1–2 attacks. Your combat rotation is 1–3 abilities, chained or spammed every 10–15 seconds. Any weapon effects that significantly change how a weapon looks or feels are locked behind a €300 pity gacha, with awful rewards that make it a money sink.
Thematically, many weapon combinations don’t make sense or have boring playstyles. Demonic twin blades that push you into rage paired with… rats? And actively using two weapons from different paths is shooting yourself in the foot.

PvE:
For some reason, the devs looked at Genshin Impact and said “that energy system limiting players from playing looks fun.”
You have an energy system that takes 3 days and 3 hours to fully charge. It caps at 500, with ~1 energy every 9 minutes. There are three forms of group PvE:

• 10-man raids: On paper, fun. In reality, rewards are capped once per week. With 9 people you know, it’s surprisingly fun to coordinate. Bosses are repetitive, sometimes buggy, and can outright kill you regardless of execution.
Don’t have 9 people? Welcome to gambling.

A large portion of players don’t read mechanics. Before fights, during fights, ever. So 10-man (and 5-man) becomes gambling on randoms knowing how to read. My success rate was about 20%. You’ll spend hours queuing, watching people die to mechanics that could be read in 30 seconds, and leaving. Rinse, repeat.

• 5-man raids: Energy-limited. Each reward claim costs 60 energy, or 180 for triple rewards, once every 20 hours.

PvE boils down to a raid every day or two, allot of gambling, and mediocre rewards.

Progression:
Probably the worst system I’ve seen in a very long time. Progression in WWM is multilayered, with each layer locked behind something more inane than the last.

Mystic skills—some of your hardest-hitting abilities—are leveled by picking flowers. Each flower has a very low chance to give 1 rare material. You need around 108 to max a skill. No markers. You just search greenery for tiny petals. The game then offers limited weekly chests and food buffs to increase drop rates. Red line painting once more.

You also need to run outposts—the third PvE mode—which offer almost no rewards besides iron for mystic skills and random gear. They scale, so you can’t prefarm. You use around 10–12 skills total, each requiring a different plant, meaning you’re farming multiple rare materials in some of the most boring content I’ve played.

Then comes gearing. You open random gear chests hoping for legendary gear with usable stats (many don’t make sense). You can spend months not getting one. Then you gamble again tuning it, needing good rolls on 6 random stat slots. Bad roll? Start over.

Lastly, Inner Ways. You can equip up to 4. They require escalating amounts of notes, awarded randomly from content chests. You constantly reroll instead of the system just not being random. They’re integral to player power, and falling behind cripples your character.

PvP:
If you’re not near central Europe, don’t bother. Above ~40 ping, input delay kills animation cancels, reactions, parries, and combos. Opponents fall out of combos due to ping differences, and you’re playing with a 1–2 second delay.

PvP also uses a separate upgrade system and Inner Ways, meaning you’re maintaining two characters and halving your progression speed.

The Story:
The story is surprisingly good—if you understand it. It follows Dark Souls-style storytelling while relying heavily on ancient Chinese history. Between awful localization and obscure references even many Chinese players don’t know, you’ll probably skip it and watch it on YouTube later.

The Content:
Global releases are slower than China’s. Level caps and progression are drip-fed every 15 days, forcing you to repeat the same progression grind. New content arrives even slower, so once you’re done, you mostly log in to dump energy every few days.

Most systems are weekly-limited. Finish them in a few hours and that’s it. Need upgrades? Too bad—weekly coin cap.
Co-op is limited, laggy, and often only counts for the host. Online presence has little point outside of dailies. This isn’t even touching on shop pricing, gacha odds, or reward quality.

The game had an insane amount of potential, but the devs keep designing great systems and then crippling them. Maybe this design works better in China, but it clearly doesn’t hit the same mark here.

I am only reviewing this as a Solo-mode player, and I will say it delivers an amazing single-player experience. I see a lot of the criticisms seem to come from PVP players, so if you are looking for a single player game, do not be discouraged, you can get so much out of this. I genuinely feel like most of the critiques that I’ve seen for this game are form people who don’t actually want to play the story quests or engage with the world, they just want the multiplayer content, which is not the bulk of the game, and are upset that the game doesn’t solely focus on PVP and multiplayer content.

If you are playing a female character, the English audio will often refer to your character as “Him/He,” even if the text will say “She/Her” (or not having a gender pronoun at all, instead having a blank space). If that is something that might be distressing to you, use the Chinese audio (better voice acting too!) or avoid the game. 

My main gripes as a solo-mode player come from decisions that I believe were made to try and attract a PVP audience. Bosses scale with your level, it is therefore impossible to raise your level and come back to a boss fight later and have an easier time beating them. Additionally, all the weapons classes are weighted for multiplayer use. And with all the different elements you need to build a set of a specific type (gear types, gears of various levels with maxed out stats for passive bonuses, leveling up the weapon skills and mystic skills specific to your gear type). That means that if you find a specific playstyle that works for you, and it’s not the weakness of the boss, you will be at a horrible disadvantage for the fight and changing out your gear will involve days, if not weeks, of playtime to build up the right set, let alone getting used to the new fighting style. It takes so much time because the weapons are locked behind progression systems designed for multiplayer games, not solo-player games, which is a bizarre choice given how most of the quests and storyline are solo-mode content to begin with. Lastly, if you want to join a sect as a solo-mode player (not the same a guild which is the multiplayer thing) to get rewards or just because it feels right to your character, you’ll probably be forced into engaging with multiplayer content if you don’t want to get auto-kicked out after a month. There is also a stock market that heavily incentivise going to other players’ worlds to take advantage of their solo-world stock market prices and other things like that which try to force single-players to engage with the multiplayer content in non-meaningful and annoying ways. 

Other than that, I honestly have no complaints. The writing for the main quest lines blew me away. I am so invested in my character’s journey to the point where I am wearing a mask in certain areas after the end of Act I to stay in character and plan outfits around sentimental outfit pieces. When it comes to quests, the only things that’s found a bit annoying as someone who is invested in my character’s story is the fact that it’s very easy to do quests “out of order” so to speak, which leads to confusing moments when the game assumes you know some lore and you don’t, or your character is going around saying their full name and where they’re from when it’s now supposed to be information they’re trying to hide. Or characters will refer to a situation that you have solved or be coy about information that you have already learnt. It is a bit frustrating, but I do understand that it gives the player a lot more freedom to run around and mess about in the world. 

I do not understand all the critiques that the quests do not have good rewards. There is so much lore to uncover in the world, even talking to characters can unlock lore nodes. I also love the Wandering Tales, which rely on you paying attention to what the characters are saying instead of just following quest marker blindly. Additionally, this game implements character stats that go up as you collect oddities (the main secret collectibles of the game). These stats will allow you to use advanced gear better, unlock passive skills, and the collectibles can be exchanged for more health, skill improvements, and some outfit pieces. In most games, they are types of collectibles just exist in a “number go up” type of way, and have no actual value to gameplay, so I find that lack of reward critique absolutely wild. I would assume they mean lack of multiplayer specific rewards. Everything you do in this game will reward you with lore, skill progression, etc. Even running around has the chance of triggering Encounter quests if the right conditions have been met, so it is worth it to travel in map instead of fast travelling. 

One feature I would love to see if taking care of horses. Riding horses is so satisfying, and I love travelling the world on horseback. The main horse that the game gives you is tied to the story and is thankfully protected form being accidentally sold, but it has zero stats for good travelling. Since there is already a house/base building mechanic, I would love to be able to build a stable and make a little home for Clip-Clop, so I know he’s doing well and safe while I am off on adventures with the beefy black horse I tamed in the wilderness (I also LOVE the horse taming feature, so much fun, there is a lot of potential here for a horse game if the devs implement a few things). 

If you are playing on the Steam Deck, the Quinghe area runs okay, but the other two areas (Kaifeng and Hexi) are too much for it.

Lastly, this game is free, so you have nothing to lose trying it out.

First of all WWM is a good game. It's got a cool Wuxia setting, action based combat with a lots of weapons to choose from, and an interesting system to drive players to interact with each other. 

However the microtransaction practices has so many predatory things about it that I can't whole heartedly recommend. It's got a lot of the red flags, multiple premium currency, you can't buy the specific amount of currency you need and different gacha with different rules that can easily mislead you. On top of all of it they're retroactively release outfits from the CN version at a far higher cost and putting it behind a misleading Gacha.'

I don't care if people don't like this review because they think I'm attacking the game. I like the game and want to support the game without feeling mislead by shady tactic. This review is here to warn people so they do not end up falling for misleading gacha tactics like many others did. To future players, especially those that never played a gacha games you should follow these rules.

- Read the details and rule of the gacha banners so you can make an informed decision. I know this sounds extremely obvious but most who don't play gacha are used to pricing transparency. Most do not expect a sudden change in rules especially between banners. 

- If a deal looks too good to be true it probably is. Check if there is something else is going on.

- Don't fall for sunk cost fallacy or fomo. They almost always bring time-limited stuff back and often easier to obtain later. 
 
For those who don't know, recently they released a new scratch (Unseen Veil) that appears to be cheap. However the price of the gacha actually jumps significantly with every scratch and many only found out after already invested a lot of money into.

Only the first scratch is 60 pearl. The price jumps significantly with every scratch. It actually adds up to 7440 pearl (over 100 USD, jumping from 60 to 180, 400, 800 all the way to 2600 pearl). It's not 7 scratch at 60 pearls each like a lot of people were mislead into thinking. You would not know this if you did not see the extremely easy to miss information in the details.

The rule is a tiny icon down near the corner for you to click on and it's even misspelled as "intro" not "info". This resulted in a lot of people to spend money on the scratch only to find out that its far more expensive than their initial price point. At lot of the time people would have already spend 30 50 dollars without said costume and will fall for sunk cost fallacy trying to finish the scratch. 

This is extremely concerning as the outfit in question CAN BE PURCHASED DIRECTLY on the Chinese server and significantly lower price too at 2580 pearl for the entire set. Meaning they made this outfit retroactively more expensive and put it behind gacha for the international release. I do not know what Netease is trying to pull but its nothing good for the long term health of the game. 

Netease is notorious for it's microtransaction practice but this was a first for me. There is more than a fair share of players who just want to enjoy the game on a budget fell for this. Why not just make the price upfront? Why resort to misleading people? You got whales spending over 40k on a ship on the 5th day of release, this isn't even about keep a game alive, your game is alive and well. Did you really have to start using this kind of tactic so soon?

You already have the legendary banner that cost over 300 dollar to hit pity (Not even the specific item you want, it's double if you want to costume), regular costumes reaching 40 USD and a bunch of other weapons skins and animation changes. Did you really have to make an existing outfit that sold for 2580 pearls and lock it behind a 7440 Gacha instead?

This is on top of the fact that the NPC for f2p or budget players to earn cosmetics is not in the international version as well as coupons being cut back from 2 a month to 1 through the login bonus. The currency for the monthly pass do not give a player to player trading currency but rather regular coins. 

Why are so many features missing and items being cut back? You can't even access some existing multiplayer function because of the missing currency.

I want to love this game, the combat is great, the world is great, the story is great, but it's this kind of practice that cause people to leave games in the first place. Most don't mind spending money on games they enjoy, most don't want to feel like they're being tricked into it.

Review written after 1,600 hours of gameplay and having experienced a wide range of situations in the game:

- Several bugs: broken world map textures, glitched interactions, bugged building items...

- Reports and bug reports are ignored: Bugs remain unresolved no matter how many times they are reported, and players reported for violations listed in the report options—including spam, inappropriate audio, cheating, and other disruptive behavior—are never punished.

- Extremely expensive cash shop: Want to look fancy? You have to pay real money to get Pearls. There is absolutely no way to earn premium currency for free (not even a small monthly allowance for F2P players).

- Instead of fixing these structural issues, every new patch just adds more cosmetics to the cash shop and shallow, cash-driven events.

- Terrible PvP system: Horrible balance that forces the player base to use the exact same rigid META builds and weapons.

- Insane lag and terrible optimization.

- Confusing UI: Cluttered menus that lack any proper explanation.

- Boring story quests: Long, tedious conversations and forced slow-walking segments that completely kill the pacing.

- Lack of content variety: Repetitive NPC models and a complete lack of voice acting.

- A Toxic Community: Because it is a free MMORPG, it attracts many toxic, weird, creepy, and attention-seeking players. The community is one of the strangest and most toxic in the MMO genre. Many guilds have an unhealthy, cult-like mindset where defending the game’s flaws matters more than criticism. Leaving a guild feels like being erased — friendships often end instantly. The game revolves around social status, creating endless drama and ego clashes.

- Global chat is constantly flooded with spam: Players beg continuously for shop outfits, Pearls, gallery exhibition votes, and sect rank votes, often repeating the same requests through unsolicited DMs. This creates an endless 24/7 scroll that makes the chat channels annoying, intrusive, and practically useless.

- A special mention goes to the Velvet Shade sect, which is by far the worst offender for community and spam issues. It embodies all of the aforementioned problems and also has a high volume of unsolicited marriage proposals and flirtatious requests that add to the overall annoyance.


Conclusion:

The game constantly tries to hook you into spending money. The shop is updated weekly with new outfits, flashy FX animations, mounts, weapon skins, and limited-time items—often wrapped in fake "special discounts" designed to trigger FOMO.

Before you play, keep this in mind:

They don't care about the community.
They don't care about optimization or stability.
They don't care about balance or fixing game-breaking bugs.
They only care about bleeding your wallet dry.

At this point, it feels less like a martial arts RPG and more like a social status simulator driven by whoever puts on the best show and spends the most money in the cash shop.

Ultimately, many players forget a harsh reality: when this pseudo-MMORPG inevitably shuts down, everything they spent real money on just to look fancy and show off will disappear forever along with the servers.

WWM impressed me with its beautiful graphics, fair monetization model, great customization options and massive amount of content. It definitely sets a new standard for free-to-play games. It takes a bit of time to wrap your head around all the pop-ups, sub-menus and different currencies, but it's well worth it once you do. 
At its core, the game is single-player and is packed with a solid main story and varied side quests. Right from level 10, you unlock two new modes: Co-op and MMO. The latter acts more like a social lobby, with both modes dedicated for group content, including dungeons and raids.
Is it a Souls-like experience? Not really, but it's close enough. The combat revolves around parries and dodges, yet it remains fast-paced thanks to the martial arts and various weapon combinations. The world map is immense and exploration is engaging with lots of minigames and secrets to discover. 
Gear progression follows a mobile-style energy system, with the energy refill not being a daily thing: this is definitely a blessing for anyone with a busy schedule since it lets you play at your own pace and still keep up. There are gacha elements in the game, but they are all focused on cosmetics items that offer no gameplay advantages.
If you're looking for a free MMO-ish game with lots of options, including both PvE and PvP, this might be your next game to try.

Where Winds Meet surprised me in the best way. The game looks and plays like a full triple A title and it is honestly hard to believe it is basically free to play. The world is stunning, the combat feels great, the character creator is outstanding and there is a huge amount of exploration and side content.

Let me point out the big things though.

First, it is not pay to win. The shop is cosmetics only. The problem is the gacha. The rates are terrible and it feels like a very old school mobile system. Some costumes have fixed prices, which is fine, but the random pulls are rough.

Second, the game throws a ton of menus, systems and features at you at the beginning. It feels overwhelming to the point of confusion. The good part is that once you get used to it, everything becomes easy to navigate. The onboarding could be much better, but you do get over that hurdle.

Now for the biggest issue I have. The leveling gatekeeping is awful. At the time of writing, I have to wait six more days to go from 55 to 60. I do not understand the logic behind this. You keep earning XP anyway, so when the gate is lifted you blast through the next levels in about twenty minutes. It makes the gate pointless. During this forced downtime I fully cleared almost the entire first zone. 98 % of all quests, exploration and objectives done. That is when it hit me. At this pace I will probably clear most of the game before I even reach max level.

After that, all that is left is a short list of activities. Five bosses per zone - Qinghe and Kaifeng, one trial, a pseudo battleground and one arena. PVP is terrible. It is a stunlock fiesta. It could have been fun, but right now it is just frustrating, although I still play it for the rewards.

I already maxed out my mastery at this level, reached almost thirteen thousand power, started collecting books for inner ways and I can already see the long term loop forming. If you remove the mini games, the game becomes three repeating activities. Farm the same bosses, farm the same arena, farm the same outpost. That is basically it.

After checking the CN version I am honestly not sure how long the game will stay alive in the West. It feels like the time gating was brought over for retention, not for any creative reason. I expected proper dungeons and raids, not just straight boss fights. The game needs engaging endgame content, not repetitive farming.

Overall I am still satisfied and I enjoy my time with it. The world and the presentation are that good. But unless the endgame improves, I worry the game will fade as fast as it appeared.

Where Winds Meet is one of those games where you start with a simple quest, and an hour later you’re standing on top of a mountain you don’t remember climbing, holding five screenshots of a random tree, and wondering when exactly your life went off-track. That’s how pretty the game is, it constantly distracts you on purpose.

The story and characters are charming too. At one point an NPC told me something deep and philosophical, and all I could think was: “Yes, wise elder, very inspiring, but could you also point me in the right direction? I’ve been lost since the tutorial.”

Exploration is where the game really shines. You start walking, notice a shiny rock, go to check it out, then find a hidden pond, then chase a butterfly, then somehow end up on top of a hill you weren’t supposed to reach yet. The game doesn’t stop you, it just silently approves your chaos.

You can interact with cats in the world, and sometimes they even pretend to like you. It’s a small, charming detail that makes wandering around even more fun, especially when they completely ignore you in the middle of a serious quest.

There are a few quirks: the pacing slows down occasionally, some objectives are explained with the confidence of someone giving directions while half-asleep, and I had a couple of small performance snags, nothing major, just small pauses for dramatic effect.

Overall though, it’s a lovely, relaxing adventure. If you enjoy exploring, getting (very) lost, and accidentally creating your own side stories, you’ll love it.

The historical references are also interesting but under-explained. For example, when the game touches on regions like the Hexi Region, it clearly expects you to already understand the significance—but for most players, there’s not enough in-game context to connect the dots. I’ve had to pause multiple times just to look up what was actually being referenced.

If the devs improve translation quality and add better historical grounding, this game goes from amazing to truly unforgettable.

Still 10/10 experience—but I’m basically playing Where Winds Meet + Wikipedia simulator at this point.

Where Winds Meet has genuinely surprised me with how much there is to do and how easy it is to get lost in the world. The open-world setting is beautiful, with some fantastic scenery, detailed environments, and moments where I’ve found myself stopping just to look around instead of rushing to the next objective.

One of my favorite parts is the freedom to switch between solo open-world play and co-op/online play. I can explore at my own pace when I want a more immersive RPG experience, then jump online when I feel like playing with other people. That flexibility makes the game feel much less restrictive than a lot of other online RPGs.

There’s also an impressive amount of variety. You’re not just running from fight to fight. There are side stories, exploration, puzzles, martial arts, different weapons and builds, NPC relationships, professions, healing, collecting, housing, mini-games, hidden areas, and all kinds of strange little encounters scattered around the world. I’m still discovering systems I didn’t even realize were there.

Combat has been fun too, especially once you start experimenting with different Martial Arts and Mystic Skills. The ability to switch styles and build a character around the way you actually enjoy playing gives the game a lot of room to grow.

It can definitely throw a lot of systems at you early on, and some mechanics aren’t explained as clearly as they could be, so there are moments where you may find yourself wondering what you’re supposed to do. But once things start clicking, the sheer amount of freedom becomes one of the game’s biggest strengths.

Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a world meant to be explored rather than simply completed. I can spend one session progressing the story, another wandering around finding secrets, and another doing side activities or playing online. Between the gorgeous world, martial-arts atmosphere, open-ended exploration, and the ability to move between solo and co-op play, I’ve been having a great time with it.

Definitely recommended if you enjoy open-world RPGs where wandering off the main road is half the fun.

While I would like to recommend this game to practically anyone, it's a matter of taste and personal preference, I can't in good faith tell anyone to play a live service Gacha Game. While the Sekiro inspired combat and Wuxia elements are fantastic, the underdeveloped MMO aspect of the game will likely wear a lot of players down over time. Three month long seasons, weak battlepass offerings, month-long stretches of time with nothing to do made up of time gated, drip fed, and buggy content that largely is comprised of mini games and weekly/daily runs of the same thing. Nearly every resource or incremental point of progress you make towards unlocking a free cosmetic/accessory is capped out. The resource farming is capped daily, coins are capped, everyday drops from monsters, crafting. I don't think there is a single system that doesn't have an internal limit to progression, even if it has no direct impact on PVE or PVP combat. I think the biggest killer of this title, for me, is the fact you run out of engaging solo content pretty early on, so you resort to trying PVP, Raids, and Abyss challenges. The raids can only be completed once per week, PVP is laggy and inconsistent (filled with bots), and the abyss trials are a fun challenge with little to no reward. Worst of all, outside of drip fed, time gated, energy capped content, is the abysmal integration of the Gacha system and no end-game trading system. I do appreciate it isn't explicitly pay-to-win, but the fact that it is so disconnected from the main gameplay loop makes it feel tacked on. Once again, you're capped to purchasing 3 premium pulls a week without forking over hundreds of dollars to get a single skin. The shop skins are 3x the price of CN servers, the Gacha is also wildly over priced (30 dollars for a single 10 pull btw) and a hard pity set at 150 which means virtually nothing. Hard pity doesn't guarantee the outfit, hitting hard pity then hitting pity again doesn't guarantee the banner reward. You have to spend on average around 400 dollars for a single item and there is no other way to purchase the premium currency without spending your college fund and selling your kidney. Here's my advice, play Sekiro, or Elden ring, Dark souls, or an actual MMO if you're into that. While I appreciate some of the potential depth of combat and the aesthetics, don't play aggressively monetized live service games like this. The lack of content, end game systems, and repetitive boring grind isn't worth it when the chance to get something good is less than .014% and the free outfits pale in comparison and take months to grind for (only because of hard caps.) I'll still revisit this game from time to time, and am willing to change my mind if the developers adapt, but I don't see that happening considering we aren't the main player-base. Until then, I'll be treating this game as if it's in maintenance mode for the next couple months (at least until Hengdao comes out.)

I have around 360 hours in this game, and unfortunately, I can’t really recommend it in its current state.

To start with the positives: the game is genuinely f2p friendly. There are no p2w mechanics, and players cannot purchase stronger gear with real money. That’s a big advantage and something more games should strive for.

However, the overall experience is held back by several major issues.

PvP feels unbalanced, and the presence of cheaters further undermines any sense of fair competition. (And no there is no skill issue or anything like that... I am quite good at PvP)
Systems like the bounty mechanic add frustration rather than meaningful engagement. U often get a bounty for no reasons, often you don't even realize when and when that happens... You will get an annoying invasion from a REAL player. Which even when u manage to defeat, u won't get anything and you still gonna have a bounty in ur head. It's better to just log off for a minute then come back to be in jail to get out, because this mechanic is really bad.
The outfit pull system also feels unnecessary and out of place, especially given how much of the social environment revolves around it. You must be very lucky to get an outfit from limited banner.

Speaking of social features, the global chat is rarely used for actual interaction. Instead, it is dominated by guild recruitment spam and players begging for outfits, which makes the game world feel less alive than it should. Even within guilds, activity tends to be inconsistent — many players join briefly, then leave or stop playing altogether. Over time, this makes it difficult to maintain any stable or active community.

While the world itself is large, there isn’t enough engaging content to support it long-term. Many events feel repetitive or uninteresting, which contributes to a gradual loss of motivation to keep playing.

For me personally, the main reason I stayed as long as I did was because I was playing with close friends. Once they lost interest and stopped playing, it became much harder to find reasons to continue. Eventually, I reached the same point.

In summary, *Where Winds Meet* has a strong foundation and a fair monetization model, but it currently struggles with balance issues, weak social systems, and a lack of engaging content. With improvements in these areas, it could become a much better experience — but as it stands now, I cannot recommend it.

I now have almost 1,500 hours of playtime, and this is probably one of the first truly negative Steam reviews I have ever written.

If you want to pick flowers, explore the world, and casually follow an AI-generated story, then go ahead and play the game.

However, if you want to do boss runs or take on genuinely difficult challenges, stay away from it.

Almost every boss is bugged, and it feels as though every animation or cutscene has the potential to interfere with the fight. The game features a challenge mode with hitless runs, which was originally the part that interested me the most.

However, you are not simply fighting the boss and learning its attack patterns. You are fighting against developers who apparently do not play or properly test their own game.

You are given unfinished bosses whose actual attacks sometimes do not match the animations being shown. Some attacks are so inconsistent and off-rhythm that it can take ten hours or more to memorize them. Not because the mechanics are particularly challenging, but because the timing, animations, and actual hit detection do not reliably match.

Once you have finally memorized every pattern, every delayed rhythm, and even every misleading animation, you still have to deal with input registration issues. The game sometimes fails to recognize that you dodged or parried an attack. During phase transitions, the fight can also freeze and prevent you from entering the second phase altogether.

The worst part is that some of these bosses have already been in the game for more than a year. Despite that, their existing issues are rarely—if ever—fixed retroactively.

The gear system is also a complete disaster. Yes, the game is not directly pay-to-win. Instead, your progress is artificially restricted by an energy system. You are only allowed to improve your equipment at the pace dictated by the game. Once you have spent your energy, it feels as though you are being starved of resources, because you may only make around two percent progress on your gear in an entire day.

At the moment, completing a single gear set takes approximately two to three weeks. I have now reached the point where I am gearing my third class. This means it takes around six to nine weeks just to build three complete sets.

And what happens after six to eight weeks? The level cap increases, and you need an entirely new gear set. Your previous set may not even be finished before you are forced to start all over again. Proper min-maxing is nearly impossible because the game constantly starves you of materials.

Class balancing also only happens roughly once every two months—if it happens at all. At the same time, there is a class called “Nameless,” which is clearly the developers’ favorite child. This class attacks safely from range, mainly uses charged attacks, and still consistently achieves the highest damage. Almost no risk, very little mechanical skill required, yet always the highest DPS.

As I said before: if you simply want to play casually, collect flowers, and explore the world, you may have a good time.

However, if you expect a fair challenge, technically polished boss fights, and reliable mechanics, stay away from this game. You are better off investing your time in a more polished game made by developers with enough experience to properly test their own content.

可以说，我已经给了这个游戏很多的机会，我用了不到60~70个小时就通关了。我真的很想想喜欢这款游戏。它画面很美，但缺点实在太多了。

我不是一遇到什么就退坑的人，但如果游戏之后继续让我失望，而且没有任何改进，我会立刻弃坑。

Very good graphics and art direction
Large amount of available content

Free to play

👎 CONS

Extremely unfriendly UI/UX, even after 100+ hours
Poor optimization for keyboard & mouse

Too many systems and items; most are confusing and unnecessary
Heavy use of caps, energy systems, and seasonal locks
Weak localization and language support
Raids with random players are frustrating and repetitive
Shop - lol


GAMEPLAY
Average overall. Expect around 150–200 hours to clear currently available content.
Gameplay revolves around blocking, reflecting, and repeating the same actions. You technically have two weapons, but in practice you use one and swap to the second only for buffs or debuffs.
The interface is one of the worst I’ve encountered in an MMO. Navigation is painful, even after extensive playtime. The sheer number of systems and items is overwhelming, and many of them never become relevant.

COMBAT
Likely enjoyable for younger players or controller users.
On keyboard & mouse, combat feels like input gymnastics rather than actual fighting. Endless key combinations, awkward positioning, and timing windows turn encounters into something closer to playing a piano than engaging combat.
Souls-like? Maybe.
Fun? Not for me — at least not on keyboard and mouse.

PvE
Some areas look great visually.
World size is below average to average, but presentation is solid.
The main story feels unfinished and abandoned.
Instances and raids are decent mechanically, but energy caps and seasonal restrictions kill momentum.
10-player raids with pugs are mostly wipe-fests. Boss mechanics are repetitive, and most players simply ignore them.
5-player content is more tolerable, depending on caps and available energy.

PvP
Not tested.Not interested in trying it on keyboard & mouse.


SOLO / CO-OP / MMO SYSTEMS
Switching between modes is buggy, annoying, and often requires unnecessary regrouping.
Ping and region differences matter a lot.
Healing bounties are nearly impossible to grab — by the time they appear, they’re already taken. Chat is constantly filled with healing requests for targets that are already healed.
Sects and reputation systems feel unrewarding compared to the time investment. Rewards (e.g. Silver Needle) don’t justify the grind.
Many progression systems are weekly capped, limiting how much you can actually play.

SHOP
The shop feels aggressive.
It’s obvious the developers are heavily pushing cosmetic monetization.
Whether that’s acceptable or not is up to the player.

FINAL VERDICT
Not recommended for keyboard & mouse players.
Where Winds Meet looks good and offers a lot of content, but poor UI design, overcomplicated combat, and heavy time-gating systems make it frustrating on PC without a controller.

Recommended if:
✔ You play on mobile or controller
✔ You enjoy grind-heavy, capped MMO systems
✔ You don’t mind messy UI

Not recommended if:
✖ You play on keyboard & mouse
✖ You value clean combat and readable interfaces
